html:
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1">
  <title>My creative coding sketch</title>
  <style>
    html, body { margin: 0; padding: 0; }
    canvas { display: block; }
  </style>
  <script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/p5@2.3.4/lib/p5.min.js"></script>
</head>
<body>
  <main></main>
  <script src="sketch.js"></script>
</body>
</html>

stages.title: Show one image
stages.subtitle: A file becomes a picture on your drawing surface.
stages.outcome: Display sample.png, then explain why its source size and canvas size are different.
stages.illustrationHint: The source picture is 320 × 240 pixels. The canvas can show the same picture at a different size.

experiment.instruction: Choose Show at 320 × 240. Then choose Show at 640 × 480. Compare the window in each picture.
experiment.expect: The displayed picture becomes smaller. The original image file stays 320 × 240.

stages.checkpoint: I can load the image, save the sketch, and explain that loadImage loads while image draws.

actions.title: Find the window and plant
actions.here: Look for the window and plant in Your sketch. Practice has already drawn the picture.
actions.editor: When you want a shareable version, use Save in p5 to open your account sketch.
actions.why: Recognizing the picture gives you a result to compare as you change the code.
actions.expect: The window, sun and plant appear on the canvas.
actions.question: What should you see at this point?
choices: A still picture with a window and plant
A new color on every frame
actions.explanation: This first sketch draws the image once.
actions.repair: In Practice, choose Run and look at Your sketch.

actions.title: Watch the picture stay still
actions.here: Look at the sun for a moment. This sketch draws the image once, so the sun stays in place.
actions.editor: Keep your saved sketch as it is. Compare its preview with this illustration. Stage 1 draws once; it does not yet animate.
actions.why: Recognize a working baseline first.
actions.expect: A still enlarged source appears.
actions.question: Should this first stage already animate for a minute?
choices: No, this stage displays the original
actions.explanation: Animation arrives in a later stage.
actions.repair: Read the Run status and first error.

actions.title: Find the image file
actions.here: Read the filename inside loadImage("sample.png"). That file holds the original 320 × 240 picture.
actions.editor: If rebuilding an account sketch from scratch, download sample.png and upload that file to the sketch.
actions.why: loadImage uses the filename to find the picture.
actions.expect: The filename in the code matches the source image.
actions.question: Does a 640 × 480 display make the source file 640 × 480?
choices: No, display size and stored size differ
Yes, displaying it doubles the stored pixels
actions.explanation: Display enlargement leaves the source unchanged.
actions.repair: Read the letters between the quote marks in loadImage.

actions.title: Name the three files
actions.here: Find sketch.js in the guide. It contains your drawing instructions. index.html loads p5, and sample.png supplies the picture.
actions.editor: If you open a p5 account sketch, its file panel lists index.html, sketch.js and sample.png.
actions.why: Each file has a different purpose.
actions.expect: You can name the page, drawing program and picture file.
actions.question: Which file will hold the drawing instructions?
actions.explanation: sketch.js contains the drawing program.
actions.repair: Read the file roles above, then find the program name ending in .js.

actions.title: See how the page starts
actions.here: Open “Explain the page setup / HTML.” Find where the page loads p5 before sketch.js.
actions.editor: For a fresh account sketch, use Copy index.html to install the supplied page setup. Practice already has it.
actions.why: index.html loads the library and sketch.
actions.expect: You can point to the script that loads p5.
actions.question: Which file loads the p5 library for the page?
actions.explanation: The script tags in index.html load p5 and sketch.js.
actions.repair: Open “Explain the page setup / HTML” and look for the script tags.

actions.title: Match the filename
actions.here: Read the quoted text "sample.png" in the loading line. Its spelling tells p5 which image file to open.
actions.editor: For a fresh account sketch, place sample.png beside sketch.js in the file panel.
actions.why: The saved project needs its own image.
actions.expect: The program asks p5 to open the supplied picture.
actions.question: For sample.png beside sketch.js, which quoted path matches?
actions.explanation: Use the project-relative filename in loadImage.
actions.repair: Check that the quoted name includes the .png ending.

actions.title: Read the loading line
actions.here: Select the line containing await loadImage. Read its meaning. The picture must finish loading before p5 can draw it.
actions.editor: Practice has the complete eight-line sketch. To keep your edited version in an account, copy your code and paste it into a duplicate.
actions.why: Loading the file makes the image available to the drawing code.
actions.expect: The name picture holds the loaded image.
actions.question: What does picture hold after await loadImage finishes?
actions.explanation: await lets the image finish loading before setup continues.
actions.repair: Read the name on the left of the equals sign, then the call on the right.

actions.title: Compare picture and canvas
actions.here: Choose Show at 640 × 480. The source is still 320 × 240. Compare the drawing size with the file size.
actions.editor: To check your shareable account version, save it in p5 and reopen its saved address.
actions.why: The canvas can display the same source at a different size.
actions.expect: The canvas is 640 × 480 and the image file is still 320 × 240.
actions.question: If loading fails, what should you inspect first?
choices: The uploaded filename and quoted path
The color mathematics from a later stage
actions.explanation: Fix missing assets before pixel mathematics.
actions.repair: Compare the first error with the filename.

actions.title: Try one reversible size change
actions.here: Select createCanvas. Choose Show at 320 × 240, then return to 640 × 480. Watch the canvas change size.
actions.editor: Change only createCanvas(640, 480) to createCanvas(320, 240), then Run. Compare the display. Restore 640, 480, Run again and Save. Explain what changed before continuing.
actions.why: One change isolates display size.
actions.expect: Smaller canvas; unchanged source file.
actions.question: What did changing createCanvas change?
actions.explanation: createCanvas changes the destination surface.
actions.repair: Restore this complete stage if syntax breaks.

vocabulary.meaning: A small p5 program. Your editor project contains the program and its supporting files.
The source is the stored picture, 320 × 240 pixels here. The canvas is the drawing surface, initially 640 × 480.
A file has a name such as sample.png. A path tells the program where that file sits inside its project.
Instructions p5 performs once when this sketch starts. Await waits for the picture to finish loading.

foundations.title: Place shapes and control drawing order
Open an image: a file becomes material

practice.task: Show the supplied image at its stored size, then enlarge its display. Describe what changed.
practice.hint: Read the final width and height arguments of image. Compare them with the image’s own dimension properties.
practice.solution: Drawing at the image’s width and height shows its original size. Larger destination dimensions enlarge the visible picture; the stored source dimensions stay unchanged. Match the width-to-height ratio to avoid stretching.

practice.task: Replace the source with your own image and keep one successful version.
practice.hint: Check the uploaded file list before editing the quoted path. A .jpg filename and a .png filename are different.
practice.solution: Upload the real file, match its exact path in loadImage, and run. If loading fails, inspect the first error and filename before changing drawing mathematics. Save the working sketch and note your source credit.

stages.idea: Your source is the material; the canvas is the surface where you arrange it. Enlarging its display does not add detail to the file.

play.try: Show the picture at 320 × 240, then at 640 × 480.
play.notice: The canvas width and height double. The source picture stays 320 × 240.

roadmap.build: Load one picture and draw it on a canvas.
roadmap.assignment: Choose a source image with your partner and name what you want viewers to notice.
roadmap.proof: Run your saved sketch and point out the difference between the image size and the canvas size.

stages.title: Make a mosaic
stages.subtitle: Read one color, draw one block, and repeat.
stages.outcome: Build a mosaic and explain how the sampling step controls its detail.
stages.illustrationHint: Each block uses one color sampled from the source. The loops visit a row from left to right, then move to the next row.

experiment.instruction: Set Sampling step to 16, then 8. Compare the same edge of the window.
experiment.expect: At 8, smaller blocks follow the edge more closely. The number of samples rises from 300 to 1,200.

stages.checkpoint: I can explain why increasing tile makes the mosaic coarser, and I saved one tested version.

actions.title: Find one block
actions.here: Look at the edge of the window in Your sketch. Each square takes its color from one place in the source picture.
actions.editor: In Practice, select const tile. It sets the distance between samples.
actions.why: Keep the sampling comparison controlled.
actions.expect: Rectangular blocks replace the smooth display.
actions.question: What does tile = 16 measure here?
actions.explanation: tile measures source-pixel sampling distance.
actions.repair: Look for a straight edge of the window where neighboring blocks meet.

actions.title: Make the invisible sampling grid visible
actions.here: Look at the block edges: they form a grid even though no outline is drawn. At tile 16, the 320 × 240 source is visited in 20 columns and 15 rows. Trace one row with your eyes, then move down.
actions.editor: Keep the program unchanged. Find noStroke(), which removes rectangle outlines. The blocks still meet along grid boundaries because rect places them next to one another.
actions.why: Reveal where samples originate.
actions.expect: Twenty block columns and fifteen rows cover the image.
actions.question: Why can you recognize a grid without drawn outlines?
choices: The filled rectangles meet along regular boundaries
The image must contain a hidden grid file
actions.explanation: The rectangle positions create the grid; outlines are optional.
actions.repair: Use tile 40 temporarily so the block edges are easier to count, then restore 16.

actions.title: Read one color and move to its neighbor
actions.here: The step selects the sampling line. In Follow one pixel, try source (0, 0), then Next sample for (16, 0). Each visit reads a color before drawing its rectangle. Stage 3 adds an address inspector.
actions.editor: Read const shade = picture.get(x, y); as “remember the color at this source location.” Read shade[0], shade[1], shade[2], shade[3] as red, green, blue and alpha.
actions.why: Read color before drawing its block.
actions.expect: You can follow a source color from get into fill and then into one block.
actions.question: What does picture.get(x, y) supply?
choices: A source color at that location
actions.explanation: get supplies the sampled source color.
actions.repair: Read the get and fill explanations consecutively with Next line.

actions.title: Follow the two loops without editing them
actions.here: Select the line beginning for (let y, then the following for (let x line. Use Next line to reach rect. Say: “choose a row, visit its columns, then choose the next row.”
actions.editor: Find the same two loops without changing them. At tile 16, calculate 320 ÷ 16 = 20 columns and 240 ÷ 16 = 15 rows. Multiply to get 300 samples.
actions.why: Columns finish before rows advance.
actions.expect: Twenty columns × fifteen rows = 300 samples.
actions.question: How many samples does this baseline make?
actions.explanation: Multiply rows by columns: 300.
actions.repair: Calculate both divisions; never set tile zero.

actions.title: Change only the sampling step
actions.here: Set Sampling step to 16, then 8. Look at the same window edge after each change.
actions.editor: Find const tile in Practice. At 8, each loop moves eight source pixels between samples.
actions.why: Change one spatial rule.
actions.expect: Smaller blocks trace the same edge with more detail.
actions.question: Which setting draws fewer blocks?
actions.explanation: At 16, the loop visits fewer places in the same picture.
actions.repair: Look at the same edge at 16 and 8.

actions.title: Explain how a source position reaches the canvas
actions.here: Restore tile 16. Select the rect line and read its explanation. x / picture.width gives a fraction of the source; multiplying by width finds the matching position on the canvas.
actions.editor: Restore const tile = 16; and Run. Work out one example: source x 160 is halfway across 320, so its destination is halfway across 640, at x 320.
actions.why: Fractions connect differently sized rectangles.
actions.expect: Source x 160 maps to canvas x 320.
actions.question: Where does source x = 160 map on a 640-wide display?
actions.explanation: Half of 640 is 320.
actions.repair: Divide first; label source and canvas widths.

actions.title: Keep one observed result
actions.here: Choose a tested tile value and write what became easier or harder to recognize. Include the setting and a specific feature, such as the doorway or plant. This is evidence for a design decision.
actions.editor: Run and Save your chosen version. Preserve its complete code before trying a different stage if you want to keep this iteration.
actions.why: Connect a decision to visible evidence.
actions.expect: A saved mosaic and actual observation remain.
actions.question: Which note can guide your next decision?
actions.explanation: Concrete observations guide further decisions.
actions.repair: Compare 8 and 40 again before writing.

vocabulary.meaning: Read a color at one chosen source location rather than drawing every original pixel.
The named source-pixel step between samples. It also determines each displayed block’s size.
An instruction that repeats while its condition stays true. The row loop contains a column loop.
A location written as x and y: x increases rightward, y increases downward, starting at the top left.

foundations.title: Place shapes and control drawing order
Sample an image: turn detail into a mosaic

practice.task: Compare tile sizes 8, 16 and 32 using the same source.
practice.hint: Change one value, run, and keep the display dimensions fixed.
practice.solution: Larger steps visit fewer locations and create larger blocks. Smaller steps retain more detail but ask the sketch to draw more blocks. Record your actual preference and what becomes obscured.

practice.task: Explain one source-to-canvas position without reading the whole formula aloud.
practice.hint: Choose a source x halfway across its width.
practice.solution: Dividing that x by the source width gives 0.5. Multiplying by canvas width places the block halfway across the canvas, even when the two rectangles have different dimensions.

stages.idea: A mosaic reads a few locations and makes a new drawing from them. Sampling distance controls both detail and the number of blocks.

play.try: Set the sampling step to 16, then 8. Look at the same edge both times.
play.notice: At 8, each block is smaller. More blocks trace the same edge.

roadmap.build: Visit the picture row by row and draw a block in each sampled color.
roadmap.assignment: Try two block sizes to see which details of your image become hard to recognize.
roadmap.proof: Save your chosen block size and describe one detail it reveals or hides.

stages.title: Find a pixel’s four numbers
stages.subtitle: A rectangular picture is stored as a long list.
stages.outcome: Choose one point in the source picture and read its red, green, blue and alpha values.
stages.illustrationHint: The mosaic can look exactly like Stage 2. The change is how the program reads colors: this stage uses picture.pixels instead of get.

experiment.instruction: Set Sampling step to 16. Choose (16, 16). Follow this point from its four values to its block.
experiment.expect: At (16, 16), RGBA is [148, 201, 207, 255]. Green is stored at address 20545 and its value is 201.

stages.checkpoint: I can calculate one pixel’s four addresses and distinguish an address from a color amount.

actions.title: Choose one pixel
actions.here: With Sampling step at 16, choose (16, 16). Find the outlined point on the source picture and its block in Teaching preview.
actions.editor: Read the selected guide line in Practice. picture.loadPixels() makes the image’s color values available to the sketch.
actions.why: Following one point connects the color numbers to a block you can see.
actions.expect: The outline marks the same sample in both pictures.
actions.question: Must a new reading method make a new visible effect?
choices: No, it can read the same colors
Yes, the picture must look different
actions.explanation: Different methods can produce matching colors.
actions.repair: Set Sampling step to 16 so the (16, 16) shortcut is available.

actions.title: Start with pixel zero
actions.here: Look at the top-left sample (0, 0). Its four color values start at addresses 0, 1, 2 and 3.
actions.editor: Find const i = 4 * (x + y * picture.width);. Substitute x = 0 and y = 0 on paper. The first red address is zero, not one.
actions.why: Array counting begins at zero.
actions.expect: First pixel addresses: 0, 1, 2, 3.
actions.question: What is the first pixel’s red address?
actions.explanation: The first array address is zero.
actions.repair: Use the inspector’s coordinate label to distinguish sample (0, 0) from a later sample.

actions.title: Calculate one later address by hand
actions.here: Choose (16, 16) again. Read the address line. It uses the source width of 320 and finds the red address 20544.
actions.editor: Calculate: 16 complete rows × 320 pixels = 5120; add x = 16 to get 5136 pixels; multiply by 4 RGBA entries to get address 20544.
actions.why: Convert pixels into channel entries.
actions.expect: Selected pixel starts at address 20544.
actions.question: Which width belongs in this source-buffer calculation?
actions.explanation: Source-buffer calculations use source width.
actions.repair: Confirm tile 16 and coordinate (16, 16), then calculate using source width 320.

actions.title: Separate the address from the amount
actions.here: Read green for (16, 16). Address 20545 holds the value 201. The address tells you where to look. The value tells you how much green.
actions.editor: Find const g = picture.pixels[i + 1];. Say: “go to the green address and remember the amount found there.” The +1 changes the address; it does not increase the green amount.
actions.why: Distinguish location from stored amount.
actions.expect: Large addresses hold values within 0–255.
actions.question: Does an address of 20545 mean a green amount of 20545?
choices: Yes, they are the same number
No, an address points to a stored amount
actions.explanation: Addresses locate values; they are not amounts.
actions.repair: Label each number “where” or “how much”.

actions.title: Read alpha and the density assumption
actions.here: Read the fourth value for (16, 16). Alpha 255 means fully opaque. This sketch uses one physical pixel per source position.
actions.editor: Keep both density lines. This starter reads source RGB and draws opaque tiles with fill(r, g, b). It does not copy arbitrary source transparency into the result.
actions.why: Image density differs from canvas density.
actions.expect: This opaque starter draws alpha 255.
actions.question: Are transparent pixels and opaque black equivalent?
actions.explanation: Transparent pixels differ from opaque black.
actions.repair: Use the supplied source for this exercise.

actions.title: Keep the original buffer unchanged
actions.here: Select fill(r, g, b). For (16, 16), fill(148, 201, 207) sets the color for the block drawn by rect.
actions.editor: Find the three channel-reading lines. There is no assignment back into picture.pixels and no picture.updatePixels() call. Reading a buffer does not require updating that buffer.
actions.why: Preserve a reliable original source.
actions.expect: Source and displayed RGB match.
actions.question: Do these reads need updatePixels to become visible?
choices: No, fill and rect draw the result
actions.explanation: Reading needs no updatePixels; drawing uses rect.
actions.repair: Restore the complete stage after accidental assignments.

vocabulary.meaning: An ordered list of numbers. Its first position is numbered zero.
Four consecutive channel amounts: red, green, blue and alpha. Alpha describes opacity.
The numbered position in the list, rather than the channel amount stored at that position.
One stored pixel per image coordinate here. This stage’s simple address formula depends on that assumption.

foundations.title: Read RGBA: four numbers make one pixel

practice.task: Calculate the addresses for (1, 1), then compare with the diagram.
practice.hint: Skip one row of four pixels, add one pixel, then multiply by four.
practice.solution: The first address is 4 × (1 + 1 × 4) = 20. Red, green, blue and alpha occupy addresses 20, 21, 22 and 23. Those addresses do not tell you their stored colors.

practice.task: Explain a pixel whose values are [100, 40, 180, 255]. Predict an inverted green channel.
practice.hint: Green is the second channel. Inversion subtracts its value from 255.
practice.solution: The transformed displayed color is [100, 215, 180, 255] if only green is inverted. Red, blue and opacity stay unchanged. Reading from the original again preserves a reliable comparison.

stages.idea: An address tells you where to look. The number stored at that address tells you a channel amount. They are different kinds of information.

learnFirst.title: Read RGBA: four numbers make one pixel

play.try: Set Sampling step to 16. Choose (16, 16), then press the right arrow on the source picture.
play.notice: The outline moves to the next block. Each block has four color values at four addresses.

roadmap.build: Find a pixel’s four color entries and draw a block using its red, green and blue.
roadmap.assignment: Trace one sampled color so you know exactly which numbers your rule can change.
roadmap.proof: For one pixel, show its four addresses and the color values stored there.

stages.title: Choose what keeps its color
stages.subtitle: A condition decides where a color rule applies.
stages.outcome: Keep a chosen left-hand region colored while changing the remaining samples toward gray.
stages.illustrationHint: focus chooses where the boundary sits. strength chooses how far the selected colors move toward their targets. Change one at a time.

experiment.instruction: Choose “Keep a region colored.” Set strength to 100%. Move the width from 40% to 70%.
experiment.expect: The color boundary moves right. More of the window keeps its original color.

stages.checkpoint: I can explain the position test and blend amount, and describe one visual consequence I actually observed.

actions.title: Find the color boundary
actions.here: Choose “Keep a region colored.” Set strength to 100% and width to 40%. Find the edge between color and gray.
actions.editor: In Practice, find const focus = 0.4 and const strength = 1. They match the two settings.
actions.why: A position test decides which blocks keep their original colors.
actions.expect: Left forty percent colored; outside gray.
actions.question: Does this rule recognize the main subject automatically?
actions.explanation: focus tests position, not object identity.
actions.repair: Confirm focus mode and strength 100%.

actions.title: Read the condition as a sentence
actions.here: Select if (x / picture.width >= focus). Read it as a sentence: “If this sample is at or beyond the boundary, use gray targets.” At focus 0.4, source x 128 is exactly on the boundary.
actions.editor: Find the same condition. The >= symbol means “greater than or equal to,” so a sample exactly at the boundary is included in the transformed region.
actions.why: Convert position to a fraction.
actions.expect: Boundary samples join the transformed region.
actions.question: At the boundary itself, does this condition select gray?
choices: No, only samples strictly beyond it
actions.explanation: The >= comparison includes equality.
actions.repair: Compare one sample’s fraction with 0.4.

actions.title: Move only the region boundary
actions.here: Keep strength 100% and change focus from 40% to 70%. Inspect which parts of the source now retain color. Restore 40% before the next experiment.
actions.editor: Change only const focus = 0.4; to const focus = 0.7; and Run. Compare, then restore 0.4 and Run again.
actions.why: Change where, not how much.
actions.expect: At 70%, more left-side samples retain color.
actions.question: What did this experiment change?
actions.explanation: focus changes a spatial boundary.
actions.repair: Check focus, then Run the edited sketch.

actions.title: Blend toward gray at half strength
actions.here: Keep focus 40% and lower strength to 50%. Look outside the retained region. Select the fill line containing lerp to connect the partial color change with the code.
actions.editor: Change only const strength = 1; to const strength = 0.5; and Run. Find paintTiles(strength): the chosen amount is passed into the drawing rule.
actions.why: Separate region selection from blending.
actions.expect: Half strength retains some outside color.
actions.question: What does strength zero display?
actions.explanation: Amount zero returns original channel values.
actions.repair: Inspect a colorful sample outside the region.

actions.title: Compare one different target rule
actions.here: Restore strength 100% and choose the invert rule. Read the regenerated targetR, targetG and targetB explanations. For any channel, the inverted target is 255 minus its original value.
actions.editor: Look at targetR in the guide code. The invert rule now uses 255 - r. If Practice has your own edits, Use lesson code loads the example there.
actions.why: Inversion chooses different channel targets.
actions.expect: Each channel targets 255 minus its source.
actions.question: What is the inverted target for a channel amount of 40?
actions.explanation: 255 minus 40 equals 215.
actions.repair: Return to focus mode for boundary control.

actions.title: Choose and record a deliberate rule
actions.here: Return to the focus rule, focus 40% and strength 100%. Write one actual comparison and what you noticed first. The rule tests horizontal position; it does not recognize objects automatically.
actions.editor: To save this version in your p5 account, choose Copy my code in Practice. Use Save in p5, duplicate your sketch, paste the code, Run and Save.
actions.why: Meaning needs an observed consequence.
actions.expect: A saved rule and specific comparison remain.
actions.question: Which statement is supported by your single viewing?
choices: Every viewer must look at the same feature
I noticed a particular feature first
actions.explanation: Your viewing supports your own observation.
actions.repair: Compare two boundaries with everything else fixed.

vocabulary.meaning: A question in code with a true or false answer. Here it asks whether a sample lies beyond the boundary.
The source-width fraction that keeps its color, initially 0.4: the left forty percent.
How far the displayed color moves toward the target: zero keeps the original; one reaches the target.
A blend between a starting number and a target number, controlled by an amount from zero to one.

foundations.title: React to the mouse and make decisions
Read RGBA: four numbers make one pixel

practice.task: Move the boundary to keep one important subject in color.
practice.hint: Look at the subject’s position as a fraction of source width, then compare before and after.
practice.solution: Choose a threshold that places the subject within the retained region. Record whether you actually noticed it earlier. The condition is spatial, so other objects in that region also retain color.

practice.task: Compare half strength and full strength without moving the boundary.
practice.hint: Keep the original source and all other settings identical.
practice.solution: Half strength mixes original channels with the gray target; full strength makes those channels equal outside the region. Note whether partial color better supports the idea than complete desaturation.

stages.idea: A condition chooses where a rule applies; strength chooses how far the rule changes each selected color.

learnFirst.title: React to the mouse and make decisions

play.try: Choose “Keep a region colored.” Set “Transformation strength” to 100%. Move “Width that keeps its color” from 40% to 70%.
play.notice: The edge of the colored region moves right. More blocks on the left keep their original colors.

roadmap.build: Keep color on the left and turn blocks beyond a chosen boundary toward gray.
roadmap.assignment: Use color to guide attention toward one part of the picture.
roadmap.proof: Point to a block on each side and explain why their colors follow different rules.

stages.title: Shape one minute
stages.subtitle: Use elapsed time to move gradually toward an ending.
stages.outcome: Turn the static rule into a sixty-second transformation that holds its final state.
stages.illustrationHint: Teaching time pauses Teaching preview at a chosen moment. Your sketch follows its own clock.

experiment.instruction: Inspect 0, 30 and 60 seconds in Teaching preview. Then choose Play actual 60 seconds and watch the full minute.
experiment.expect: Progress is 0, 0.5 and 1 at those checkpoints. After a minute, constrain keeps progress at 1 and the ending holds.

stages.checkpoint: I can explain elapsed progress and final strength separately, and I watched a real full-minute run.

actions.title: Pause at 30 seconds
actions.here: Move Teaching time to 30 seconds. Teaching preview holds that moment. Your sketch follows its own clock.
actions.editor: In Practice, find let start and draw(). They let Your sketch keep time as it draws.
actions.why: The slider lets you inspect the middle of the minute.
actions.expect: Teaching preview shows the halfway point. Your sketch keeps its own time.
actions.question: Does moving Teaching time change the clock in Your sketch?
actions.explanation: Teaching preview and Your sketch have separate clocks.
actions.repair: Look for the paused label on Teaching preview.

actions.title: Locate where the clock starts
actions.here: Select if (start === undefined), then start = millis(). Use Next line to reach the progress calculation. The start reading is assigned on the first draw frame and retained on later frames.
actions.editor: Keep this first-frame condition inside draw. Moving the start assignment into every frame would keep resetting elapsed time; moving it into async setup can conflict with this p5 version’s startup clock reset.
actions.why: Avoid the p5 v2 startup-clock reset.
actions.expect: Later frames keep the original start.
actions.question: Should start be reassigned on every frame?
choices: Yes, so it always stays current
No, retain the original starting reading
actions.explanation: Repeated resets would prevent elapsed progress.
actions.repair: Restore the first-frame condition if progress stalls.

actions.title: Inspect three states without waiting
actions.here: Set Teaching time to 0, then 30, then 60 seconds. Compare the three states. Calculate t = elapsed milliseconds ÷ 60000 before checking the displayed fraction.
actions.editor: Find constrain((millis() - start) / 60000, 0, 1). Leave the actual run and divisor unchanged while inspecting the teaching states.
actions.why: Inspect states without claiming elapsed viewing.
actions.question: What progress should remain after seventy seconds?
actions.explanation: constrain holds the ending at one.
actions.repair: Choose one Teaching time value at a time and compare the displayed progress with seconds divided by 60.

actions.title: Distinguish progress from final strength
actions.here: Set Teaching time to 30 seconds. Lower strength from 100% to 50%, compare, then restore 100%. At t = 0.5 and strength = 0.5, the drawing amount is 0.25.
actions.editor: For one experiment, change only const strength = 1; to 0.5 and Run. Read paintTiles(t * strength). Restore 1 before continuing. The divisor remains 60000.
actions.why: Progress and strength control different quantities.
actions.expect: Half strength ends halfway after sixty seconds.
actions.question: Does half strength shorten the duration?
choices: Yes, it finishes in thirty seconds
No, it changes the endpoint amount
actions.explanation: Strength changes endpoint, not duration.
actions.repair: Check that the divisor remains 60000.

actions.title: Use a quick rehearsal correctly
actions.here: Move Teaching time quickly from 0 to 60 to rehearse the sequence of states. This is a quick inspection, not a full-minute viewing. Read the generated progress line: its divisor remains 60000.
actions.editor: Keep the divisor at 60000. If you manually tried a shorter duration such as 6000, restore 60000 before saving or presenting. Controls on this page do not edit your online sketch.
actions.why: Quick inspection differs from full pacing.
actions.expect: You can inspect the ending quickly while the copied program still uses 60000 milliseconds.
actions.question: Does quick inspection with Teaching time export a shorter sketch?
choices: Yes, inspection changes the exported duration
actions.explanation: Teaching inspection and the exported elapsed-time program serve different purposes.
actions.repair: Inspect and restore any manually changed divisor.

actions.title: Watch one real minute and record it
actions.here: Prepare notes for the beginning, middle and ending. A quiz answer or a scrubbed image does not count as watching the whole experience. Record what you actually see and when you see it.
actions.editor: Press Run and start a separate timer as the image appears. Watch sixty seconds and a few seconds beyond. Confirm the ending holds, record actual timestamps and Save the working version.
actions.why: Measure the visible experience directly.
actions.expect: The ending holds beyond sixty seconds.
actions.question: What verifies the pacing more directly?
choices: Counting a requested number of frames
Watching a full run with a separate timer
actions.explanation: Frame-rate requests do not guarantee elapsed duration.
actions.repair: Time from visible start; inspect a stalled clock.

vocabulary.meaning: The function p5 calls repeatedly to make visible frames.
One thousandth of a second: 60000 milliseconds is sixty seconds.
The current clock reading minus a remembered starting reading.
The fraction of the minute completed, constrained between zero and one. It is multiplied by strength.

foundations.title: A real minute: turn elapsed time into a color journey

practice.task: Try a six-second rehearsal, then restore the assignment duration.
practice.hint: Change the duration setting rather than the pixel or color formulas.
practice.solution: Six thousand milliseconds compresses the same progression for inspection. Restore sixty thousand, replay, and verify a complete minute before presenting.

practice.task: Keep a full-minute duration but reduce the final transformation strength.
practice.hint: Scale the amount passed to the blend, leaving the clock calculation alone.
practice.solution: A final strength of one-half covers only half the color journey over the same minute. Compare whether the quieter endpoint communicates your intended change.

stages.idea: Time progress and transformation strength are separate values. A minute can travel toward a subtle endpoint or a dramatic one.

learnFirst.title: A real minute: turn elapsed time into a color journey

play.try: Move Teaching time to 0, 30 and 60 seconds. Then choose “Play actual 60 seconds” to watch the full minute.
play.notice: Teaching preview pauses at each selected moment. Your sketch follows its own clock.

roadmap.build: Use a clock to change the colors over one minute, then hold the ending.
roadmap.assignment: Shape the beginning, middle and end of a silent one-minute piece.
roadmap.proof: Watch one full minute and note what you see at the start, halfway through and at the end.

stages.title: Replay and present
stages.subtitle: Make the same journey work again at the viewing size.
stages.outcome: Restart by clicking and check the composition in wide and narrow viewports.
stages.illustrationHint: This stage uses the viewport dimensions. A click restarts its clock. The starter stretches to fit; wide and narrow previews help you notice that design choice.

experiment.instruction: Compare the wide and narrow preview widths, then click inside the running p5 canvas after it has changed.
experiment.expect: The drawing follows the viewport and its proportions can change. Clicking returns the color journey to its beginning.

stages.checkpoint: I tested replay and resizing, then opened and watched my actual saved presentation link.

actions.title: Change the viewing shape
actions.here: Choose Wide preview, then Narrow preview. Watch the picture fit the new space in Teaching preview.
actions.editor: In Practice, find createCanvas(windowWidth, windowHeight). It uses the width and height of its own window.
actions.why: The same sketch can be shown in windows with different shapes.
actions.expect: The canvas changes shape with the preview.
actions.question: What changes when you choose Narrow preview?
choices: The shape of the teaching canvas
actions.explanation: The program fits its canvas to the available window.
actions.repair: Choose Wide preview again to compare the two shapes.

actions.title: Compare three moments
actions.here: Inspect 0, 30 and 60 seconds in Teaching preview. Repeat the three times and look at the same detail.
actions.editor: Keep your project unchanged during this comparison. Note the same three moments you will look for during full runs.
actions.why: Check matching states under unchanged rules.
actions.expect: Matching teaching times show matching states; Restart p5 starts a new actual preview.
actions.question: Does Restart p5 on this page also save your online editor project?
choices: No, editor saving is a separate action
actions.explanation: The local preview and your saved editor project are separate.
actions.repair: Compare source, settings and selected sample first.

actions.title: Restart the actual sketch with a click
actions.here: Select the mousePressed explanation. Let the actual p5 preview change, then click inside its canvas. Watch the return to original colors before the journey develops again.
actions.editor: Click your running sketch’s canvas after it has progressed. Restart your separate timer. Repeat once with the same source and rule, then compare matching moments.
actions.why: Restart timing without changing source.
actions.expect: Clicking the sketch begins its journey again.
actions.question: What needs resetting for this default replay?
actions.explanation: The unchanged source needs no restoration.
actions.repair: Click the canvas; verify mousePressed exists.

actions.title: Test a wide and a narrow window
actions.here: Use the wide and narrow preview widths. Inspect the window, plant and edges. Select resizeCanvas(windowWidth, windowHeight), then the rect line. The source fractions adapt positions, but independent width and height can stretch shapes.
actions.editor: Resize your browser or editor preview and inspect the actual sketch. Decide whether stretching suits your idea. Record any presentation size that makes important content hard to read.
actions.why: Check composition in real presentation spaces.
actions.expect: The canvas fits; proportions may stretch.
actions.question: Does filling any viewport automatically preserve image proportions?
choices: Yes, every aspect ratio stays identical
No, this starter stretches to fit
actions.explanation: Independent width and height can distort proportions.
actions.repair: Record the failed size before revising layout.

actions.title: Open the actual presentation link
actions.here: Keep your notes ready for a link check. This local illustration demonstrates the mechanism; it cannot verify the asset paths or latest saved version of a separate online project.
actions.editor: Save. Use File → Share to obtain the actual fullscreen link and open it in a new tab. Keep the sketch-code link separately. Verify that the intended image and behavior load.
actions.why: Verify the actual share destination.
actions.expect: Saved fullscreen page loads the intended sketch.
actions.question: What is the strongest check of the fullscreen link?
choices: Open the exact link and watch it
Assume the workbook preview proves it
actions.explanation: Only opening a link checks its destination.
actions.repair: Verify assets, Save, and reopen the link.

actions.title: Rehearse twice and preserve the result
actions.here: Record two full presentation rehearsals and any resizing issue. The starter uses no randomness. The optional seeded extension remains available in the foundations if your own concept needs it.
actions.editor: At the intended display size, watch two complete silent runs and restart deliberately. Save the tested version and preserve its full code. These checks do not replace the class’s required iterations and observations.
actions.why: Test the complete presentation twice.
actions.expect: Matching moments repeat with unchanged inputs.
actions.question: Are randomSeed and noiseSeed interchangeable?
choices: No, each controls its own generator
actions.explanation: Each seed controls its own generator.
actions.repair: Compare inputs; restore the simple working version.

vocabulary.meaning: The available browser page area. windowWidth and windowHeight describe its current size.
Restart the clock while keeping the same source and visual rules.
A named function, windowResized, that p5 calls when the available page size changes.
The editor’s shareable presentation-page link. It differs from the code link and from the browser’s own fullscreen mode.

foundations.title: Place shapes and control drawing order
React to the mouse and make decisions
Transform a drawing without damaging its source

practice.task: Replay twice and compare three matching moments.
practice.hint: Keep the source and controls fixed. Use the same elapsed-time positions for comparison.
practice.solution: The default starter should reproduce its displayed states at matching progress values. If results differ, inspect changing inputs or state that was not reset before adding more effects.

practice.task: Test the actual fullscreen link and resize the browser.
practice.hint: Check important edges, labels, background and source proportions.
practice.solution: Adjust proportional placement where necessary. A viewport-sized canvas does not itself invoke browser fullscreen; the shared fullscreen presentation page must also be tested.

stages.idea: Repeatability includes source material, timing, procedural choices and human actions. Seeds address only the procedural generators they control.

learnFirst.title: Place shapes and control drawing order

play.try: Choose Wide preview, then Narrow preview. Choose “Replay from the start.”
play.notice: The canvas fits the narrower space. Replay sends the clock back to the start.

roadmap.build: Click to replay the minute and resize the canvas to fit the window.
roadmap.assignment: Use the fullscreen link to rehearse the same silent piece twice at presentation size.
roadmap.proof: Open the shared link, resize the window and compare the two runs at the same moment.

stages.title: Refine and document together
stages.subtitle: Turn a working mechanism into an observed creative project.
stages.outcome: Preserve real experiments, timed observations, collaboration and checked submission links.
stages.illustrationHint: The starter code is the same as Stage 6. This stage adds your creative decisions, genuine iterations and documentation; a new visual effect is not required just to show progress.

experiment.instruction: With your partner, preserve one version, change one rule, save the new version and watch a whole minute. Compare your independent notes before deciding what to revise.
experiment.expect: You have a specific changed rule and an actual observed result. Continue until the assignment’s full iteration, viewing and documentation requirements are satisfied.

stages.checkpoint: I checked the live assignment against actual work, tested every submitted link and named any remaining work honestly.

actions.title: Compare two versions
actions.here: Choose A, then B. Look at the same window edge in Teaching preview. Both versions show 30 seconds.
actions.editor: With your partner, follow the Week 9 brief to explore all linked Color Theory examples. Record two or three observations from what you see.
actions.why: Comparing the same moment makes a change in block size easier to see.
actions.expect: B shows smaller blocks than A. Keep your own observations for the class record.
actions.question: What counts as completing the example exploration?
choices: Both partners working through all linked examples
Selecting the answer on this card
actions.explanation: Answering cards does not perform class activities.
actions.repair: Finish all actual examples together before claiming completion.

actions.title: Agree on a concept and divide real responsibilities
actions.here: Open Finish and expand Concept and partner. Together, name your source, intended alternative reality and first rule to test. Divide concrete independent work, then agree when to reunite and compare.
actions.editor: Save a baseline version both partners can identify. Preserve each person’s actual tested variation or agreed contribution before discussing the results.
actions.why: Make contributions and shared decisions visible.
actions.expect: Named roles precede actual contribution records.
actions.question: Which record describes collaboration accurately?
choices: What each did alone and what you decided together
actions.explanation: Specific records show how collaboration shaped work.
actions.repair: Assign concrete tasks and reunite to compare.

actions.title: Preserve at least three algorithm iterations
actions.here: Open Finish and expand Iterations. For each version, record the rule changed, your prediction, what actually happened and the next decision. Keep the source and settings identifiable. Blank rows are not evidence of completed work.
actions.editor: Develop, test and preserve at least three algorithm iterations. Save the complete code for each before replacing it. Copy sketch.js here supplies a starting program; your tested changes make the iterations.
actions.why: Connect changed rules with observed results.
actions.expect: Three preserved tested algorithm versions exist.
actions.question: Which is useful iteration evidence?
choices: A saved changed version plus its observed result
Three planned filenames with no tested sketches
actions.explanation: Planned filenames alone are not iterations.
actions.repair: Recover overwritten versions or test another honestly.

actions.title: Watch at least three full runs with a timer
actions.here: Open Finish and expand Full-minute viewings. Prepare rows for viewing number, actual timestamp, what you noticed and your interpretation. Keep each partner’s initial attention notes separate before discussing them.
actions.editor: Watch at least three complete runs with a separate timer. Restart deliberately, keep the project silent and record real moments. Inspecting a few slider states does not replace watching the entire minute.
actions.why: Watch pacing, not just isolated states.
actions.expect: Three full viewings have real timestamped observations.
actions.question: Can inspecting 0, 30 and 60 seconds on a slider replace a full viewing?
choices: Yes, those three states are enough
actions.explanation: Scrubbing cannot replace complete timed viewing.
actions.repair: Label interruptions and watch another full run.

actions.title: Compile the class spreadsheet and write the process blog
actions.here: Compile real iterations and observations in the class spreadsheet linked from the live assignment. Use the full workbook’s blog outline to organize collaboration, experiments, timed observations, credits and related projects.
actions.editor: Choose the iteration you will post, Save it and verify its title and links. Preserve other versions so your blog can show meaningful differences.
actions.why: Prepare evidence for actual submission destinations.
actions.expect: Spreadsheet and blog contain real process evidence.
actions.question: Do downloaded local logs replace the class spreadsheet?
choices: No, compile the requested material there too
Yes, downloading the blank files submits it
actions.explanation: Local templates do not replace class submissions.
actions.repair: Consult live instructions for unclear destinations.

actions.title: Check the actual blog, code and fullscreen links
actions.here: Open Finish and use Links and the self-checklist to audit actual deliverables: blog, sketch-code link, fullscreen link, source and inspiration credits, collaboration record, iterations and timed observations.
actions.editor: Open the exact saved code and fullscreen links. Check the intended image and behavior, then rehearse two silent runs at presentation size. Repair any failed link or unintended sound before submitting.
actions.why: Check what your intended viewer opens.
actions.expect: All three links reach intended current artifacts.
actions.question: What proves a link is usable?
choices: Its label looks complete in a note
Opening the exact link and checking the result
actions.explanation: A candidate URL needs actual destination verification.
actions.repair: Repair failed links, Save, and test again.

actions.title: Finish separate preparation and make an honest final audit
actions.here: Return to the live assignment for separate sound preparation, its specified reading or exercises and the actual deadline. List completed evidence and remaining work. Mark a learning checkpoint only when you can support it with your own work.
actions.editor: Keep this one-minute project silent. Save after tested changes and retain a backup of the exact code and image used by the submitted version.
actions.why: Audit real work without invented completion.
actions.expect: Required evidence and separate preparation are accounted for.
actions.question: Does separate sound preparation change this project’s silent requirement?
choices: Yes, add sound to satisfy it
actions.explanation: Sound preparation remains separate; this artifact stays silent.
actions.repair: Name missing work and complete the actual activity.

vocabulary.meaning: A preserved version with a deliberate rule change and a record of the result you actually observed.
What you noticed and when. An interpretation explains what you think that observation means.
An honest account of what each partner did independently and what you decided or tested together.
An item the assignment asks you to submit, such as a process blog, code link or fullscreen link.

foundations.title: Practice: find the first error and repair one thing

practice.task: Run one honest iteration-and-viewing cycle with your partner.
practice.hint: Choose one rule change, save it, watch the full minute, and write actual timestamps.
practice.solution: Record the changed rule and its observed effect. Compare your separate attention notes before agreeing on a revision. Repeat until you have at least three iterations and three full timed viewings; one cycle alone is incomplete.

practice.task: Audit the submission from the viewer’s perspective.
practice.hint: Use the project checklist, open every link, and check the class spreadsheet destination.
practice.solution: Verify the blog, code and fullscreen links; source and inspiration credits; collaboration record; color observations; iteration evidence; and timed viewings. Rehearse two silent runs. Fill gaps with real work rather than invented documentation.

stages.idea: A useful process record lets someone connect a decision, a changed rule and an observed result. Your partner can help question that connection.

learnFirst.title: Practice: find the first error and repair one thing

play.try: Compare A (16) and B (8), both paused at 30 seconds. Save your own versions and watch each full minute for your class notes.
play.notice: B shows smaller blocks than A. The clock stays at 30 seconds, so you can compare the same moment.

roadmap.build: Use the same program as Stage 6 while you test and document it together.
roadmap.assignment: With your partner, save at least three iterations and watch the piece for a full minute at least three times.
roadmap.proof: Share your process and links on the blog and enter your changes and timed observations in the class spreadsheet.
